title: Frederick Douglass Visits His Old Master
text:
Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland and escaped in 1838. In his writings he described Thomas Auld, his legal owner, as cruel and hypocritical, and in 1848 he published a stinging open letter to him. In 1846 British friends had bought Douglass's freedom from Auld's brother Hugh, to whom Thomas Auld had transferred him.

In June 1877, by then a famous orator and United States Marshal for the District of Columbia, Douglass returned to St. Michaels, Maryland. Thomas Auld, old and near death, had let it be known that he wished to see him, and Douglass went to his bedside. In Life and Times of Frederick Douglass he describes the meeting. Auld called him Marshal Douglass; Douglass asked to be called Frederick, as in the old days, and addressed him as Captain Auld. The old man wept, and Douglass was for a time too moved to speak. They talked frankly. Auld told him that in Douglass's place he would have run away too. Douglass also corrected one charge he had made in print about Auld's treatment of his grandmother, after learning he had been mistaken.

The visit was widely reported, and some critics thought Douglass had been too soft on a former slaveholder. In his account he made clear that his hatred of slavery had not changed. He now saw Auld, as he saw himself, as a victim of the circumstances of birth, law and custom.
lesson: You can make peace with a person without excusing the wrong he took part in. Forgiveness and moral clarity are not opposites.
source: Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881), Part 2, chapter on the visit to St. Michaels
